4.t: EDITORIAL
What made September '71 different from all other Wah Yan Septembers was the
coming into being of Pun U Association Wah Yan Primary School. It is situated at
Shiu Fai Terrace which is not far away from the mother school. More about Pun U
Wah Yan in the pages that follow.
There were a number of staff changes：
Mr. Choy Heung Ming Joined the staff in September 1971, taking the place of Mr. Chan
Kim Man who went to Canada for further studies.
Mrs. Cissy Lau, because of family affairs, gave up fultime teaching but continued as
form-mistress on a part-time basis. She was replaced Miss Agness Cheung Yuen
Har in September 1971.
Mr. Bosco Cho, a past student, Joinea the staff in February 1972 on a temporary basis.
Mr. Vincent Lee was selected to study the special third year mathematics course at
Northcote College of Education. During his absence his place was taken by Mr.
Johnson Liao, also a past student.
Gary Lam, who had joined the staff early in 1971 left us at the end of December and
went to Australia.
The night school carries on with some difficulty and with a reduced number
of Classes. Girls are now admitted ana there are now a good year but there are reasons
to hope for a brighter future.
On December 2Ist the Wah Yan Jesuit Community Sufferes the loss by death of
one of their members Father Sean Turner. A great many past students mourn the
passing of one whom they rightly regarded as a great scholar.

5.t: Examination Results
The matriculation examination results for this year were good. Fifty-five stu-
dents entered for the Matriculation Examination and 52 matriculated.
Twenty-five
distinctions and sixty-nine credits were gained. Thirty students were admitted to Hong
Kong University and one to Chinese University. Five went to universities abroad.
The School Certificate Examination results were satistactory. 152 students enter-
ed for the Examination, obtaining 35 distinctions and 433 credits. One student was
awarded a Government Scholaship for the Matriculation Course.
The 45th Anniversary of the founding of our Wah Yan 15th Hong Kong finds the
group in a flourishing condition. Wah Yan is indeed fortunate in having among its old
boys such devoted and competent scout officials as Philip and Stephen Ching and
Geoffrey O'Young who have for many years given of their best to train succeeding
generations of Wah Yan Scouts. The Club Section of the 15th Hong Kong is centred
at Pun U Wah Yan and has already proved its mettle by winning the Bishop's Shield.
On the sports side it has to be said that things are not as they used to be in the
great days gone by.
Only our gallant C Grade Basketballers saved us from complete
oblivion. We are not, however, going to weep about our misfortunes. We are planning
for better things in the future.
It is possible that the zeal and effort that formerly went into games and athle-
tics is now being diverted into other channels, important in their own way. Our Judo
Club is 4½ years old and green belts have begun to appear on all sides. A new Bowl-
ing Club has been founded and in a competition reached the quarter-final. Our Red
Cross Cadets have increased their numbers. The Life Guard Club, now a solia 14 years
old patrois popular beaches and most usefully trains its members to life-saving.
The Christian Life Community tries to instil in the members the desire to lead
a full christian life by self-sanctification and apostolic work. This needs leadership
training which entails lectures and seminars. An enclosed retreat is also part of the
training that our members took part in. They also took part in a summer camp and
in bazaars and fun fairs run for the underprivileged. And our members took part in
a Vocation Month inspired by the Hong Kong Serra Club, an organization where many
of our past find an outlet for their zeal.
The Social Activities Club is meant to bring home to its members, the social
needs of the Community that they are part of. It also tries to give them the opportu-
nity to do something practical about those needs.
The members have taken part in
various useful activities such as fun fairs, fund raising and running a Summer Camp
for our adopted school in the New Territories- and that is planned for the coming

14.t: Rev. Fr. John Turner, S. J.
Father Turner died at Wah Yan College on Dec. 2lst 1971, aged 62. He had been on
our teaching staff from 1951 until 1954 and again from 1962 until 1964 when ill health
compelled him to give up teaching. He was a learned man in the lore of East and West
and as will be seen on other pages in this issue was not only a poet but also an artist.

munity Work, Public Assistance, and

Social Weltare Ofhcer （salary scale $1,550

social work qualification function in
varlous settings as caseworkers，
g9rOuP
workers or community workers. Ofhcers
who have a degree not in social work will
receive in-service training in the Depart-
ment and may later on have the oppor-
tunity to obtain professional training in a
University.
The Department employs as Welfare
Assistants school leavers who have a Hong
Kong Certifcate of Lducaton. The salary
scale is $600 - $1,400 with the prospect of
promotion to Principal Welfare Supervisor
whose salary starts from $1,475 and goes
up to $2,050. The Welfare Assistants may
work in most of the Department's Divisions

assistance workers, members of the welfare
in rehabilitation centres and com-
munity centres.
The other category consists of the
Welfare Supervisors who join the Depart-
ment at the minimum age of 25.
In
addition to a Hong Kong Certificate of
Education, they are required to have some
experience in teaching or working with

engaged in correctional institutions to
work with Juvenile delnquents In groups
Their salary scale iS $875 - $1,400, with

cipal Welfare Supervisor.
Students who are to matriculate and
who are interested in going into social
work as a career should consider profes-
sional education

now

Social work

people or feeling sorry for them
To be a soclal

be genuinely_ interested in people，
convinced of the dignity and worth of
the individual, respectful of every one's
right to live his own Iife and to make his

terment and justice is also essential. The
chooses social work as

career must be able to establish relation-
ships with all kinds of people and to be
in Contact with human suffering and with

normal experience.
This requires well-
balanced men and women with consider-
able courage, tact and patience.

166.t: DRUG ADDICTION-a problem of youth
Drug addiction has been recognised as
a social problem in many advanced indus-
trial societies such as the U.S.A.and
Britain. These countries have witnessed
an increase in the number of drug addicts
in recent years, especially among youths.
The problem clearly alarms the public and
the law - enforcing agencies alike - and
if nothing effective is done to check the
worsening of the problem, a section of our
youths will easily be ruined by drugs.
Until recently, drug addiction was still
primarily a problem of middle-aged per-
sons rather than youths. This was so even
in the sixties and so we can find support-
ing evidences in many countries of the
world. Thus about 10 years ago, of the
reported active narcotic addicts in the
U.S.A.， only a few percent were middle-
aged.
Many of them had acquired the
habit when they were young men after
their migration to Hong Kong.
But now drug addiction has become
the problem of youths today. The point
is that during the past few years there is
a rapid rising proportion of youth addicts
being reported in many countries.
Why is it that drug addiction is
rapidly becoming a problem of youth：
Criminologists and sociologists have to
account for youthful addiction - but we
need not concern ourselves with such
high-level explanations. What we should
note is that youths often take drugs De-
cause of their inability to resist the mira-
culous effects that drugs are purported to
offer to their consumers. As such, they
become the prey of their own curiosity.
Youths are often lured to believe that
drugs are able to relieve pain, keep on
alert and make one feel happy. Such
experiences, nevertheless disappear when
drugs are not. And in order the consumer
can have these experiences again, it is
necessary to take drugs once more and in
increasing doses.
The result is that the
person will soon get addicted in this way.
Recently, the death of a student be-
cause of his addiction raised a public
outcry that efforts must be made to pre-
vent youth from being addicted. At the
same time, the incident also showed that
drug addiction among youths in Hong
Kong is a fact that we cannot deny any
longer. We need not overemphasize the
consequences that endure if drug addic-
tion were to spread to our youths - tor
they must be clear enough for every citizen
of Hong Kong who is concerned about the
welfare of his children. We should see
that adequate measures are adopted to
check the menace before it is too late.We
still have time to prevent our youths from
being corroded by the damaging effects of
drugs, but success will depend on whether
we can stop the drug traffic effectively.
The success of the measures we take will
have to depend on the co-operation and
support that citizens of Hong Kong are
willing to ofter to the government. But
if such assistance is forthcoming, there is
no reason why drug addiction as a youth
problem cannot be tackled effectively.
